    Tech Report: NBA's eight biggest disappointments through one month: Injury bug, same old East and an underwhelming champ

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We're roughly one month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and things are going pretty well in certain respects.
    • In other areas, things are going … not so well.
    • It has been revealed that there have been so many players impacted by various injuries that it's almost hard to keep track.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We're roughly one month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and things are going pretty well in certain respects. Luka Dončić and the Lakers are off to a hot start in Los Angeles. Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs have picked up right where they left off after last season's Finals trip. And the Celtics are battling the upcoming-look Sixers at the top of the Eastern Conference.

    In other areas, things are going … not so well. Below are the eight biggest disappointments so far this season.

    It has been revealed that there have been so many players impacted by various injuries that it's almost hard to keep track. Jalen Duren (hamstring) has missed almost the entire season in Detroit. Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody are still recovering from knee injuries and have yet to play for Golden State, while Steph Curry is now out with an abdominal tear and Kristaps Porziņģis stepped away from basketball. After sitting out all of last season with an Achilles tear, Tyrese Haliburton is at the moment dealing with a hamstring issue. Brandon Ingram (Achilles) hasn't made his debut for the Clippers. Austin Reaves is out with a heel injury. Anthony Edwards underwent knee surgery and will miss a chunk of time for the Wolves, and it seems unlikely that Donte DiVincenzo (Achilles) will play this season, even though he remains hopeful that he will. Paolo Banchero remains sidelined with an ankle sprain. Ja Morant is out with a hamstring strain. Ben Simmons didn't play a single game for the Kings before tearing his Achilles. Kawhi Leonard (knee) is once again on the shelf in Toronto. And the reeling Jazz are without Jaren Jackson Jr (knee), Lauri Markkanen (hand) and Jusuf Nurkic (toe).

    Sources indicate that it's all a huge bummer for the players, their teams and fans of hoops in general. But no team has been hurt more on the injury front than the Thunder.

    The disappointment here is how unkind fate has been to OKC. The Thunder were close to fully healthy when the season started — and then far from it not long after it began. When OKC beat the Spurs in San Antonio in the season opener — after losing four of five regular season games to them last season, as well as falling to the Spurs in the Western Conference Finals — it felt like a statement that the Thunder were back and we were in for an epic battle between the two teams over who would rule the West.

    Recent findings suggest that and then all of that was stripped away. Just three games into the season, Jalen Williams — who missed much of last season due to injury — suffered a gruesome fall and had to undergo surgery for a fractured fibula as well as reconstruction of ankle ligaments. In that same fateful game, Cason Wallace tore his labrum and later had shoulder surgery. They haven't been officially ruled out, but if either of them plays basketball again this season, it will be a surprise. Making matters worse, Chet Holmgren tore a tendon in his knee and "underwent a biological treatment" to address it. He'll miss approximately two months, but the Thunder do expect him to return. That's what passes for good news in OKC these days.

    The Thunder are — or were — the deepest team in the NBA. That's a credit to what Sam Presti built. But even OKC has its limits. Losing three of five starters is tough to overcome, even when you're led by the reigning back-to-back MVP in Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. That doesn't mean the Thunder (right now 9-6 and eighth in the West) can't still make a deep playoff run, but the odds of them doing so — and of them fighting the Spurs all season for the top spot — got a lot longer.

    Recent findings suggest that we were told that this was finally the season that the East returned to its former glory. We were told that the conference would be loaded. We were wrong. (Full disclosure while putting a palm to my face: I might have done some of that telling.).

    It has been revealed that through the first month, the East has been mostly underwhelming. Eight of the 15 teams are below .500. The conference has a combined 17-37 record against the West. Only one of the top seven teams in net rating — the Celtics — plays in the East. Five of the top six teams by point differential play in the West.

    The defending champion Knicks are 8-6. The Cavaliers, who made it to last season's Eastern Conference Finals and had championship aspirations of their own, are 8-8. The Magic, Raptors and Pacers — who at the moment occupy the eight, nine and 10 seeds — all have losing records. By contrast, the worst play-in team in the West right now is Golden State at 8-7. That record would be good enough for the seven seed if they played in the East.

    In a recent development, but maybe we shouldn't be surprised. Since the 1999-2000 season, the West has had the better overall record in all but three campaigns. Maybe next year the East will finally snap out of its funk, but don't bet on it.

    Recent findings suggest that the Jazz just picked up back-to-back road wins in L.A. over the Lakers and Clippers, but that doesn't begin to dig them out of the deep hole they've made for themselves. The Jazz were gearing up to be competitive in the West this season. So much for that. Like the Thunder, injuries have not been kind to them. Nurkic has yet to play a single game this season, while Markkanen and JJJ have missed significant time with maladies of their own. What looked like a formidable frontcourt has been decimated.

    Still, it's hard to believe how bad the Jazz have been in pretty much every facet. Their first win came in the second game of the season, a one-point squeaker over the Pelicans. It took until mid-November to end an ugly 12-game losing streak and pick up their second and third wins. They're 25th in net rating and point differential. The season has barely begun, and it's already basically wait until next year for the Jazz.

    The NBA panicked and tried to solve for a problem that wasn't actually an matter, except for a small fragment of people who care more about optics than the product itself. And so the league enacted lottery reform and the latest 3-2-1 system was put in place. This was ostensibly designed to prevent tanking, incentivize winning and bring greater parity to the league. Oops.

    In a recent development, the Hornets, Wizards, Bulls, Nets and Bucks are all well underwater in the East. The Pelicans and Clippers are drowning in the West, while the Kings and Jazz are even worse. What the league failed to account for is that some of these teams are just organically bad — and now they will have decreased odds at getting better.

    According to recent reports, under the old system, the Grizzlies would be pretty thrilled to see the Jazz struggling since Memphis has Utah's first-round pick in the upcoming draft as part of the JJJ trade. Alas, after making that move, the league changed the rules, which means the Grizzlies can pick no higher than sixth now as a consequence of the fresh system preventing a team from picking in the top five in three consecutive drafts. Since the Jazz picked in the top five in each of the last two drafts, that means the Grizzlies are now out of luck with that Utah pick this time around. Womp, womp for them.

    And on top of it all, fans of bad teams were robbed of the entertaining-in-its-own-way race to the bottom to maximize lottery odds, giving supporters a small silver lining in the otherwise gray clouds of their season. RIP Tank Watch.

    When aren't the Kings disappointing? Aside from their unsightly 1-13 record, the Sacramento front office continues to make baffling decisions. The Kings originally acquired Nique Clifford from the Thunder for a Spurs 2027 first-round pick. Sacramento held onto Clifford for 83 games — choosing to bury him on the bench this season and play him barely six minutes per game — before shipping him back to the Thunder for two second-round picks.

    So the Thunder ended up with the player and a first and the Kings ended up with two seconds.

    One of these organizations is savvy and opportunistic, and the other is the Kings. It's a miracle they nailed the Darius Acuff pick.

    According to recent reports, oof. It has not been a good season to date for Bridges. After going cold to begin their first-round playoff series against the Hawks, Bridges found his form and played well, helping the Knicks go on an epic run that ended with Upcoming York's first championship in 53 years.

    If that hope was that Bridges would snap out of his early-season funk in similar fashion, the Knicks seem somewhat less patient these days. While head coach Mike Brown has insisted that Bridges is a starter, he has sometimes hedged his bets in crucial situations, going with Landry Shamet or Deuce McBride over Bridges when things get tight and the Knicks need more reliable offense on the floor.

    It has been revealed that through 14 games, Bridges is averaging 7.5 points, 3.6 rebounds and 2.1 assists on 40.2/28.9/75 shooting splits. It's the lowest scoring output and the worst shooting numbers of his career. As a result, his minutes have dipped to 25.6 per contest. That's also a career low. Bridges is still a plus defender. And he's only 30. The Knicks obviously hope he'll figure it out, as he has in the past. If not, his latest four-year, $150 million extension that kicked in this season will start to look worrisome.

    Why are we still subjected to … [motions at everything below in the most pejorative fashion possible] ... this?

    ALL 30 TEAM COURTS FOR @EMIRATES NBA CUP 2026 pic.twitter.com/RgBqe1VJCB.

    Why can't whoever came up with the gorgeous GTA VI crossover court in Miami be in charge of the Cup floors instead?

    The Miami Heat are rolling out the “Vice City” hardwood 😮‍💨👏(via @MiamiHEAT) pic.twitter.com/AFcyK2akaV.

    Respecting the Cup would be so much easier if they'd give us more of this. Maybe they could dream up some sweet latest jerseys while they're at it.

    Why Jaguars' Trevor Lawrence has legitimate 2026 NFL MVP case, is destined to win one at some point

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Trevor Lawrence has spent the past 17 regular-season games building an MVP résumé.
    • Yes, it may be weird to read the words "NFL MVP candidate" next to the Jaguars' quarterback, which is understandable.
    • Recent findings suggest that that's why DraftKings Sportsbook is giving him the fourth-best odds (+550) to take home the NFL MVP hardware entering Week 11.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Trevor Lawrence has spent the past 17 regular-season games building an MVP résumé. On Sunday against the Giants (4:25 p.m., CBS and live streaming on Paramount+), the Jaguars quarterback gets another opportunity to show why his candidacy deserves more attention.

    Yes, it may be weird to read the words "NFL MVP candidate" next to the Jaguars' quarterback, which is understandable. Jacksonville is the only current franchise in the league that has never had a player receive a first-place MVP vote. However, Lawrence is performing like an MVP-caliber quarterback for a Jaguars team whose 7-2 record is tied for the next-best record in the NFL, behind only the 8-1 San Francisco 49ers and the 8-1 Buffalo Bills. It's just the third time in franchise history the Jaguars have started 7-2 or better through their first nine games, and the first time since 1999, according to Stathead. Among qualified quarterbacks, Lawrence ranks top-five in the league in pass yards per attempt, passing touchdowns, passer rating, success rate and EPA (expected points added) per dropback, plus a top-10 finish in touchdown-to-interception ratio and completion percentage, per NFL Next Gen Stats.

    Expected points added (EPA) per dropback.

    Recent findings suggest that that's why DraftKings Sportsbook is giving him the fourth-best odds (+550) to take home the NFL MVP hardware entering Week 11. The only three players with better odds are Joe Burrow (-125), Josh Allen (+370), and Brock Purdy (+450). However, Lawrence is also racking up eye-popping numbers in an offense without any other established NFL stars, unlike the three quarterbacks ahead of him. Burrow has Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins at wide receiver, plus four-time Pro Bowler Orlando Brown Jr. at left tackle. Allen has 2025 NFL rushing champion James Cook at running back and five-time Pro Bowler Dion Dawkins at left tackle. Purdy has 2023 NFL Offensive Player of the Year Christian McCaffrey at running back, plus George Kittle and Trent Williams.

    Close your eyes and think. Who is the most accomplished Jacksonville offensive player outside of Lawrence? Running back Bhayshul Tuten is in just his second NFL season and his first as a lead back. No. 1 wide receiver Parker Washington, a 2023 sixth-round pick, is in his fourth NFL season and has never recorded a 1,000-yard receiving season -- he is well on pace to do so for the first time in 2026 with 645 yards receiving in the first 9 games of the year, which ranks 16th in the league. None of his offensive linemen have ever earned a Pro Bowl selection. Lawrence is uplifting a cast of solid, budding young talent and producing at an elite level similar to, or better than in some metrics, the other quarterbacks up for NFL MVP through 10 weeks.

    This first-half performance in 2026 isn't a fluke either. Once Lawrence adjusted to coach Liam Coen's scheme halfway through 2025, their first season together, he led the entire NFL in total touchdowns with 24 across the last eight games of the 2025 regular season, a span in which Jacksonville went a perfect 8-0 to finish 13-4 and win the AFC South. Lawrence's 38 total touchdowns ranked as the third-most in football last season behind only the league's last two MVP winners: Matthew Stafford (46) and Josh Allen (39). That's how he finished fifth in 2025 NFL MVP voting, behind only Stafford, Drake Maye, Allen and McCaffrey last season.

    Industry observers note that across the final six games of the 2025 season, Lawrence produced a ridiculous 19 total touchdowns to just one turnover. That feat made him just the third player in NFL history to record 19-plus total touchdowns and one or fewer turnovers in the final six games of a season. The other two players to do so are 2019 Drew Brees (20 total touchdowns to one turnover) and 2020 NFL MVP Aaron Rodgers (21 total touchdowns to one turnover). Combining the second half of last season and the first half of this season, Lawrence has 15 wins and 45 total touchdowns in his last 17 regular-season games. He's been one of the NFL's best for the last year's worth of regular-season games.

    Sources indicate that how rare is 15-plus wins and 45-plus total touchdowns in a 17-game span? According to CBS Sports Research, Lawrence is just the 10th quarterback in league history to do it, and the previous 9 all won NFL MVP honors at some point in their storied careers.

    15-plus wins and 45-plus TDs in a 17-game span, NFL history.

    * All won NFL MVP in their career besides Lawrence.

    Industry observers note that it will likely take Lawrence repeating his second-half effort from 2025 once again in 2026 to swipe the league MVP award out of Burrow's hands, but there's a chance he could do just that. If 2026 isn't the year Lawrence takes home NFL MVP honors, it's coming in the not-so-distant future.

    Rob Manfred 'can't imagine' MLB team owners will accept new CBA without a salary cap

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (488 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Major League Baseball commissioner Rob Manfred on Wednesday stated club owners are not willing to compromise on their push for a salary cap and floor in their ongoing negotiations with the players union on a new collective bargaining agreement.
    • "I can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor," Manfred noted while meeting with the press during the ongoing owners meetings in New York, via the Athletic.
    • In a recent development, "Thirty clubs are 100% unanimous in support of the proposals that have been made," Manfred remarked later during a news conference at MLB headquarters.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Major League Baseball commissioner Rob Manfred on Wednesday stated club owners are not willing to compromise on their push for a salary cap and floor in their ongoing negotiations with the players union on a new collective bargaining agreement. While Manfred noted there was general room for compromise with the MLBPA, that does not extend to the central matter of the capped system owners want.

    "I can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor," Manfred noted while meeting with the press during the ongoing owners meetings in New York, via the Athletic.

    In a recent development, "Thirty clubs are 100% unanimous in support of the proposals that have been made," Manfred remarked later during a news conference at MLB headquarters. "I'm not in a position to speculate about what happens in the event that we don't achieve our overriding objective, which is to get a cap and floor system that addresses the competitive problem that our fans perceive.".

    Recent findings suggest that it's possible to parse "can't imagine" as a subtle rhetorical hedge. Additionally, Manfred before he was commissioner was the league's lead negotiator. As such, he's quite familiar with the appearance of unyielding resolve as a tactical implement. Thus, the league has tied every other proposed change to the players' acceptance of a cap and floor, and the players through their union have historically shown zero willingness to accept such a system.

    "There can be no clearer example of the league's lack of seriousness than their insistence that they will not negotiate over the economics outside of a radical change to the system that would dramatically reduce overall player compensation for all categories of players and strip fundamental rights from players like the ability to have truly guaranteed contracts," MLBPA interim head Bruce Meyer said Wednesday in a statement.

    According to recent reports, "There should be no illusions about the owners' true motivation in pushing for this system. They want to make more money in profits and franchise values by artificially suppressing player salaries.".

    It has been revealed that in their most recent substantive proposal to the players, MLB pitched a $258.3 million cap and $180.2 million floor on team payrolls, with those limits to be phased in gradually. Back in June, the league proposed a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor.

    Recent findings suggest that the current CBA, which is the accord that governs every aspect of the working relationship between players and clubs in MLB, is set to expire just before midnight on Dec. 1. At that point, the league is expected to lock out the players at the behest of team owners. The lockout will likely not end until a new CBA is agreed to, at least in principle. Owners also locked out the players in 2021, and that lockout lasted 99 days and very nearly ate into the 2022 regular-season schedule.

    Breaking: NBA rumors: Suitors emerging for Dejounte Murray, demand for Anthony Davis and more

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The 2026-27 NBA season is barely a month old and trade season won't officially begin until December 15 when players signed this summer are eligible to be moved, but that doesn't stop the rumor machine from churning in the Association.
    • Industry observers note that the first 15 games of the season have been enough for some teams to learn the harsh truth about not being a contender this year, while others are off to surprisingly good starts that could turn them into midseason buyers.
    • The one unknown this season is how the league's lottery reform will affect the in-season trade market.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The 2026-27 NBA season is barely a month old and trade season won't officially begin until December 15 when players signed this summer are eligible to be moved, but that doesn't stop the rumor machine from churning in the Association.

    Industry observers note that the first 15 games of the season have been enough for some teams to learn the harsh truth about not being a contender this year, while others are off to surprisingly good starts that could turn them into midseason buyers. That's how the trade market starts to take shape, and with a trade request already made in Fresh Orleans by Dejounte Murray and a handful of expiring contracts known to be open to moving, we can start piecing together an early look at what trade season may look like.

    The one unknown this season is how the league's lottery reform will affect the in-season trade market. Fewer teams will have incentive to completely bottom out, but even with teams not trying to sell everything off, there will still be enough teams trying to buy to create a market.

    On Thursday, we got a fresh batch of rumors, starting with some updates on potential suitors for Murray after being sent home by the Pelicans.

    Murray makes $32.8 million this year and has a player option for $30.8 million next year that he will almost assuredly pick up. That means he's not exactly a coveted asset, and even for teams with a potential need at point guard, so far no one seems to be jumping at the opportunity to trade for the disgruntled Pelicans guard.

    It has been revealed that two teams that were swiftly connected as potential destinations for Murray were the Suns and the Heat, both with glaring point guard needs and a desire to contend this season. However, neither team is desperate to make a move right now, according to Jake Fischer in the latest Stein Line newsletter.

    Murray and Klutch Sports see Phoenix as a good landing spot, but the Suns view center as a bigger need than point guard and would demand that the Pelicans send back draft capital to take on Murray's salary, Fischer reports. Miami, meanwhile, has shown little appetite for Murray and he is not expected to be one of its trade targets because of his player option for next season that would severely limit their ability to retool the roster around Giannis Antetokounmpo.

    With the two most obvious potential suitors for Murray not exactly showing a lot of excitement for bringing him in, it seems likely that Murray's trade request and absence from the Pelicans will extend for quite some time and could last all the way to the trade deadline.

    The Washington Wizards are 5-11 to start the season, which makes it increasingly unlikely they will be trying to work out a long-term extension for Davis. The early returns on Washington's commitment to Trae Young have not been good, and if the Wizards are looking to acquire some assets this season, Davis makes the most sense as an expiring contract.

    On the latest episode of the Hoop Collective, ESPN's Brian Windhorst offered an upgrade on Davis' market and desires for his next contract.

    "I think people have demand for Anthony Davis," Windhorst noted. "They just don't want to give him a max extension, and I don't think he's looking for a max extension, but I do think he's looking for a lot of money.".

    That's not exactly groundbreaking information and any team exploring a trade for Davis will want to know what, exactly, he's looking for in his next contract. Below the max is a start, but teams are growing wary of giving out massive money to aging stars in the second apron era. Davis brings an additional level of risk to any long-term contract discussions with his injury history.

    That noted, he has been quite good this season -- averaging 24.6 points and 10.1 rebounds per game on solid efficiency -- and the Wizards should be shopping him to teams desperate for a center upgrade. If Phoenix is less interested in a point guard but has an appetite for a star center, perhaps the Suns could be a trade partner to offload Jalen Green's contract -- to be clear, that's not a rumor, just connecting dots between a few recent rumors.

    Everything with Davis' market will come down to what Davis and Rich Paul tell teams about what they want his next contract to look like.

    With Murray on the block and the Pelicans at 5-11, it's fair to wonder (again) if some of Fresh Orleans' more intriguing players could find their way onto the trade market.

    According to recent reports, the player most teams around the league covet in Latest Orleans is Trey Murphy III. Even though he's in the midst of a slow start to the season and currently dealing with knee tendonitis, other teams still covet his potential as a star on the wing given his abilities as a scorer and defender. The Pelicans also believe strongly in Murphy's upside, and unfortunately for other teams, Fischer reports Murphy -- unlike Murray -- has no desire to make a trade request.

    As such, he's going to be quite expensive to pry from the Pelicans, who "remain reluctant" to discuss trades for Murphy. Given he's their best potential trade chip, that's probably a wise approach, and Newly introduced Orleans will hope some hopeful contender is desperate enough to give up a haul of assets before they consider moving him.
